title: EWAT: early warning and anomaly typing for microservices
tagline: Tells harmless drift (a load ramp) apart from a real failure in microservice metrics, then names the failure type.
problem: Microservice metrics drift all the time: traffic ramps, scale-ups and deploys move every distribution. A plain drift detector turns each of these into an alert, so on-call engineers learn to ignore it. EWAT asks two questions instead: is this change harmless, and if not, which kind of fault is it?
approach: A two-sample MMD test with random Fourier features compares a reference window with the last five 30 s steps of a 6-service × 17-feature signal; its threshold is the 99.5 % quantile of normal-regime MMD². When the gate opens, an STGCN encoder over the call graph and a Siamese projection embed the window and a Mahalanobis classifier types it. Drift typed harmless for 6 steps replaces the reference (look-through) without alerting; a fault confirmed for 2 steps raises a typed alert.

demo.caption: `ewat demo` computes live on a seeded synthetic episode (no cluster data): MMD drift score per step, the traffic ramp typed as harmless drift and absorbed, then a latency fault on the `ad` service raising a fail_slow_latency alert 120 s after onset; the timeline chart follows.

limits: Synthetic faults are clean and their classes are known at training time; the numbers show the pipeline works, not production accuracy.
Slow resource leaks look like drift: 24 % are missed within the 15-minute fault phase and the median delay is 630 s.
On the internal cluster, the look-through drift/fault separation (H2) failed on ~21-step episodes; it has not been re-validated on real data.
The demo model is trained on synthetic data only and the API expects 6 services × 17 features.
role: Sole developer. Built during my ML research internship at Devoteam (AIOps), where it is used internally.
